results.title: Wicked VFX breakdown
results.brief_description: Doctor Dillamond anchors Wicked’s emotional arc, awakening Elphaba’s sense of justice. To create his expressive digital presence, Framestore studied a goat named Summer, observing breathing, chewing, ear flicks and facial movement, while drawing on Peter Dinklage’s performance.
results.description:
Doctor Dillamond is central to Wicked’s emotional arc. As Elphaba’s history professor, he helps awaken her sense of justice, so his digital presence needed to feel real and expressive.
Framestore built the CG character through close, practical research. Artists visited a goat sanctuary, using a goat named Summer as the blueprint for Dillamond’s body, movement and behaviour. They studied breathing, chewing, ear flicks and facial motion, while also drawing on Peter Dinklage’s voice performance.
The result balances animal and actor: a believable goat with enough human feeling to carry one of the film’s key emotional relationships.

results.title: Frog Detective 3: Corruption at Cowboy County
results.brief_description:
The third and final game in the Frog Detective trilogy finds mystery in Cowboy County, where Frog Detective joins the ‘number-one detective’, Lobster Cop, to solve the case of some stolen hats.
Worm Club combines the series’ usual detective work with the sights and sounds of the Western, as players interview and help a new cast of absurd townsfolk and outlaws. Cowboy County is bigger than the earlier games’ settings, with “vast and rough” terrain to cross. What began as a gag became one of the game’s key features: a scooter system developed by Tom Bowker, turning movement itself into part of the joke.

results.title_for_label: Frog Detective 2: The Case of the Invisible Wizard
results.description:
Another mystery is afoot in Frog Detective 2: The Case of the Invisible Wizard. In the town of Warlock Woods, a parade welcoming the Invisible Wizard has been mysteriously destroyed. As the ‘second-best detective’, players interview a new cast of low-poly characters and follow clues through gentle, comic conversation.

This second instalment expands the series’ play style with a detective notebook, letting players track interviews and mark residents as suspicious. Composer Dan Golding also develops the game’s playful jazz score, adding different instruments as Frog Detective meets each character. The result is a mystery shaped by humour, rhythm and care.

results.title: Frog Detective 1: The Haunted Island
results.brief_description:
In Frog Detective 1: The Haunted Island, the stereotype of a hard-boiled detective becomes a friendly frog investigating a ghostly noise. Developed by Grace Bruxner while she was still studying game design, this first game in the Frog Detective trilogy turns detective fiction into a silly, kind-hearted adventure.
It borrows from screen mysteries like Agatha Christie’s Poirot (1989), using familiar music, camera angles and episodic structure. But the mystery is deliberately low-stakes, and the detective is polite, enthusiastic and apologetic when suspicious. Through comic dialogue and absurd interviews, Bruxner finds humour in making noir softer, stranger and much more charming.

constellations_other.name: Animal hijinks
constellations_other.description: As long as stories have been told on screen, audiences have loved films, TV shows, memes and videogames about animals being naughty. This constellation shares some key examples of animal comedy throughout the ages.

results.title: [5 Couleurs de France]
results.brief_description:
This film is a TV Color Paris production titled ‘5 Couleurs de France’, which translates as ‘5 Colours of France’. It features a presentation on the 1967 Cannes Film Festival, with a voiceover spoken in English. The 1967 festival was the 20th anniversary of the festival. The film includes snippets of interviews with Claude Lelouche, Sylva Koscina, Robert Bresson, Monica Vitti and Vanessa Redgrave, translated by the narrator.

It also contains footage of film stars and directors at the festival, particularly at the awards ceremony. These include guest of honour Brigitte Bardot, award presenter Virna Lisi and winner of the Palme d’Or (then known as the Grand Prix International du Festival) Michelangelo Antonioni, for his film ‘Blow Up’.

The colour is faded throughout the film.

results.title: The Cute Machine
results.creator_credit: Martine Corompt and Australian Film Commission
results.brief_description:
The Cute Machine is an exploration into the morphology of cute characterisation and iconography and its relationship to the biological world, seeking to analyse this ‘Cute ideal’ by correlating it with the Zoological process known as Neoteny

The CD contains two sections that had already been exhibited as installations (Sorry! and Activity Station) but were then adapted to a screen version. The remaining sections elaborate on the themes of cute iconography and its analysis.

The Cute Machine proposes an environment where cute iconography and user friendliness have rampantly accelerated, and reduced computer interface design to the look and sophistication of an infant toy, while also taking the premise, Cute = young to the extreme, where the ‘Cutest’, becomes an abstracted mutation of the original sentiment.

constellations_primary.name: From cute to evil
constellations_primary.description: In The Cute Machine, players are rewarded by making characters with the most juvenile or baby-ish features. Explore how broader screen works uphold or disrupt the idea that characters with cute traits are inherently good and those without are evil.

results.description:
Artistic videogames are becoming common, but they’re not a new phenomenon. In the 1990s, Australian artist Martine Corompt made videogame artworks that blended biological theory with technological development to explore the concept of cuteness. One aspect that Corompt investigated is ‘neoteny’, a term that describes how some species retain juvenile, ‘cute’ traits in adulthood to make others feel protective of them.

She drew a parallel between neoteny and the changing aesthetic of tech in the 90s. Her early artworks were made on Amiga, but she noted that Apple computers began introducing faces to their interface in the 90s, and messages addressing the user directly, creating a sense of familiarity — the computer wasn’t just a tool, but a friend.

The Cute Machine morphs and mutates ‘cuteness’ to the extreme, blurring the boundaries between innocence and transgression.

Please be advised, this work contains cartoon violence, nudity and adult themes.

results.title: Bluey mini-figurines
results.brief_description:
First launched in 2019, Bluey mini figures turn moments from the animated series into small objects made for play and collecting. Measuring around 6 to 8 cm, the figures are designed to fit pre-schoolers’ hands, allowing children to hold, arrange and replay familiar scenes and imagine new ones.

Many figures refer directly to specific episodes, from Bluey and Bandit’s cook-off in ‘Pavlova’ to the playful family routines of ‘Bin Night’.

Together, they show how screen characters move beyond the frame. Mass-produced and widely available, these toys carry Bluey into everyday play, family life and global popular culture.
